rows.question: What is the main claim of this piece, and where is it argued?
rows.text:
The main claim is that most published research findings are false — stated outright early on: "It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false" [spya-xpu5tw], a line repeated again a few paragraphs later [spya-zjrg6r].

The argument runs in stages through the piece:

1. A mathematical model, using a 2×2 table comparing claimed findings to true relationships in a field, derives the "positive predictive value" (PPV) — the chance a statistically significant finding is actually true — from study power, significance level, and the ratio of true to false relationships being tested [spya-hjja9x].
2. This model is then extended to include bias (research practices that manufacture significance even when it shouldn't exist) [spya-j7femp spya-s46ctb], and the effect of many independent teams testing the same question [spya-zjre9m spya-u5x4p2].
3. From these formulas, six corollaries are drawn — smaller studies, smaller effect sizes, more tested relationships, more design flexibility, more financial/other interests, and "hotter" fields with more competing teams all make a finding less likely to be true [spya-vzv8aq spya-p2upz7 spya-f65pfg spya-hkh8ey spya-s4b0q7 spya-mgrr58].
4. A worked genetics example and simulations across study types [spya-c5mfye spya-y0a3ah spya-umhdpk] are used to show PPV commonly falls below 50% in real research settings.
5. The piece then argues that in "null fields" with no true effects at all, claimed findings simply measure the prevailing bias rather than any real relationship [spya-pw5xz4 spya-khfp04 spya-x7m59a].
6. It closes with proposed remedies: bigger, lower-bias studies, registration of trials, and more honest accounting of pre-study odds [spya-t4k903 spya-a2jbw9 spya-fa6b0w spya-mjwvkp].

rows.question: What does the paragraph beginning “Corollary 1: The smaller the studies conducted in a scientific” mean?
rows.text:
That paragraph says small studies are less trustworthy than large ones. In the article's terms, a small study has less statistical "power" — a weaker ability to detect a real effect if one exists — and as power goes down, the positive predictive value (PPV, the chance that a claimed finding is actually true) drops too [spya-vzv8aq]. The article states this directly: "Small sample size means smaller power and, for all functions above, the PPV for a true research finding decreases as power decreases towards 1 − β = 0.05."

It then gives a concrete contrast: findings are more likely to be true in fields that run large studies, such as randomized trials in cardiology with several thousand subjects, than in fields with small studies, like most research on molecular predictors, where sample sizes are about 100-fold smaller [spya-vzv8aq].

My inference is that this is the first of the article's six corollaries building directly off the earlier mathematical argument — having shown algebraically that PPV falls as power falls, the author is now translating that into a practical rule of thumb: all else equal, trust results from big studies more than from small ones.

rows.question: Which paragraph gives the strongest support for the central claim, going only on the piece itself?
rows.text:
My inference is that the strongest support is the paragraph summarizing the simulation results across study designs, since it turns the abstract PPV formula into concrete numbers showing how rarely findings clear 50% true: a well-powered randomized trial starting at 50% pre-study odds comes out true about 85% of the time, but exploratory epidemiology studies may be true as little as one in five times, and massive discovery-oriented testing (e.g., 30,000 genes tested against 30 true ones) yields an extremely low probability of truth for each claim [spya-umhdpk].

This paragraph is doing the real argumentative work because it's where the earlier algebra (the PPV formula derived from power, bias, and the ratio of true to false relationships) actually gets applied to realistic research scenarios, letting the reader see the "most findings are false" conclusion fall out as a near-universal result rather than just a formal possibility. The worked example in Box 1, where a genome-wide association study's post-study probability of truth barely rises above 0.1%, functions similarly but as a single illustrative case rather than the general sweep across fields [spya-c5mfye spya-y0a3ah spya-uvmvbc].

rows.question: What does the author mean by positive predictive value?
rows.text:
In the article, positive predictive value (PPV) is the probability that a research finding claimed as statistically significant is actually true, once the study has been run — it's described as "the post-study probability that it is true" after a finding crosses the significance threshold [spya-hjja9x].

The article derives it from a 2×2 table comparing claimed findings against the real, "gold standard" truth in a field, combining three things: the pre-study odds that a relationship is real (R, the ratio of true to false relationships being tested), the study's statistical power (1 − β, its ability to detect a real effect), and the significance threshold (α, usually 0.05) [spya-hjja9x]. The formula given is PPV = (1 − β)R / (R − βR + α) [spya-hjja9x], and the piece later extends this same PPV concept to account for bias and for multiple competing research teams [spya-gfvava spya-j7femp spya-zjre9m].

So in plain terms: PPV here answers "if a study reports a positive result, what's the chance that result is really true, rather than a false positive?" — not the accuracy of the test in general, but specifically of findings in that paper being correct.

rows.question: What is the main claim of this piece, and where is it argued?
rows.text:
The piece's main claim is that most published research findings are false — stated directly in the title and abstract, where the author writes that there is increasing concern that most current published research findings are false, and that it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true across most study designs and settings [spya-rupg9e].

The argument runs in several stages. First, Ioannidis builds a formal model: the probability that a research finding is true depends on the prior probability of it being true, the statistical power of the study, and the level of statistical significance, from which he derives the positive predictive value (PPV) of a claimed finding [spya-hjja9x]. He then extends that model to add two further distorting factors: bias in how studies are run and reported [spya-j7femp spya-s46ctb], and the effect of many independent teams testing the same question, which further drives down the PPV of any single "first" finding [spya-zjre9m]. A worked numerical example (a genome-wide association study for schizophrenia) is given in Box 1 to show the math in practice [spya-c5mfye spya-y0a3ah spya-uvmvbc].

From this framework he draws six corollaries about when findings are less likely to be true — smaller studies, smaller effect sizes, more and less-selected tested relationships, more design flexibility, more financial/other interest, and "hotter" fields with more competing teams [spya-nx5jjr spya-vzv8aq spya-p2upz7 spya-f65pfg spya-hkh8ey spya-s4b0q7 spya-mgrr58]. The argument is then summarized quantitatively in a simulation table showing that in the described framework, a PPV exceeding 50% is quite difficult to get [spya-umhdpk], before he closes with proposals for improving the situation [spya-t4k903].

rows.question: What does the final paragraph of the article say?
rows.text:
The final paragraph argues that most new discoveries will keep coming from hypothesis-generating research with low or very low pre-study odds, so a single study's statistical significance only gives a partial picture without knowing how much other testing has happened in the field. It notes that despite a large statistical literature on corrections for multiple testing, it's usually impossible to know how much data dredging preceded a finding — and even knowing that wouldn't reveal the pre-study odds. So, Ioannidis concludes, researchers are stuck making subjective but still useful assumptions about how many tested relationships are likely to be true in a given field, drawing on the wider field and on biases seen in neighboring fields, to properly interpret and contextualize research claims [spya-y44q7p].

rows.question: What is the main claim of this piece, and where is it argued?
rows.text:
The piece's central claim is that people can't think clearly about anything that has become part of their identity, so the way to have better ideas is to keep that identity as small as possible [spya-xv45wq]. It's argued in three steps:

First, the author notices that religion and politics produce uniquely bad arguments compared to topics like Javascript or baking, and traces this to the fact that these topics let people argue from mere conviction rather than expertise [spya-znm6fz spya-pfruy3 spya-dpvyy2]. He then rules out the idea that it's because these topics have no definite answers, since some political questions do have definite answers and still degenerate into shouting [spya-ah2ape spya-gv44uj].

The real cause, he argues, is identity: a topic becomes unarguable once it gets tangled up with who people think they are, and this depends on the people, not the topic — a Bronze Age battle is safe to discuss, a modern political one isn't, because "no one would know what side to be on" [spya-kwzcxp spya-uz3ta2]. He extends this with the programming-language example, where identifying as an "X programmer" turns a real, answerable question into a holy war [spya-s6tp4k].

From there he draws the practical conclusion that gives the essay its title: since any topic can become unarguable once it's part of your identity, the fix is to minimize how many things you let into your identity in the first place [spya-zdmhnz spya-xv45wq spya-nt9xpg].

rows.question: What does the paragraph beginning “More generally, you can have a fruitful discussion about a” mean?
rows.text:
That paragraph generalizes the point just made about programming-language debates: a conversation can go well only if the topic doesn't touch any participant's sense of self [spya-zdmhnz]. Politics and religion are especially dangerous not because of what they're about, but because they happen to be wrapped up in so many people's identities — yet the same piece notes you could still discuss them productively with someone who doesn't personally identify with a side [spya-zdmhnz]. The paragraph then flips the usual assumption: even a topic that looks completely safe, like which is better, a Ford or a Chevy pickup truck, can turn into an unproductive fight if it happens to be bound up in that particular listener's identity [spya-zdmhnz].

My inference is that the paragraph is doing the work of separating "topic" from "identity" as causes: it's arguing that whether a discussion stays rational depends on the people in it, not on some property of the subject itself — which sets up the essay's closing move, that the fix is to keep as few things as possible tied to your own identity [spya-xv45wq].
